blocks.text: In positive feedback the response speeds up the controlling system. During childbirth, when the uterus begins to contract, sensory neurons signal the hypothalamus, which triggers the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin makes the uterus contract more and more strongly; the hypothalamus receives the message of stronger contractions and triggers more oxytocin. The series continues until the baby is born.

In negative feedback the end product stops the first step of the process; it is common in the endocrine system. When blood glucose rises above normal, beta cells of the islets release insulin, which lowers it; once glucose is back to normal, the normal level stops the beta cells releasing insulin. Likewise, when blood glucose falls, alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it; the normal level then stops the release of glucagon.

blocks.alt: Top: a positive feedback loop: the uterus contracts, sensory neurons signal the hypothalamus, the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, and a red arrow returns to stronger contractions and more oxytocin until the baby is born. Bottom: normal blood glucose in the centre; a rise after a meal leads beta cells to release insulin, which returns glucose to normal; a fall during fasting leads alpha cells to release glucagon, which returns it to normal.
blocks.caption: Positive feedback of oxytocin, and negative feedback of insulin and glucagon (original diagram after Figures 16.7 and 16.8).
blocks.long_description: In positive feedback the response speeds up the process that produced it: contractions of the uterus during childbirth lead, through the hypothalamus, to oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which causes stronger contractions and more oxytocin until the baby is born. In negative feedback the end product stops the process: high blood glucose makes the beta cells release insulin, glucose falls to normal and the normal level switches insulin release off; low blood glucose makes the alpha cells release glucagon, glucose rises to normal and glucagon release stops.

blocks.prompt: You studied all day and skipped breakfast and lunch. Which hormone rises, and how does feedback end its release?
blocks.explanation: Glucagon from the alpha cells rises because blood glucose is low; it releases glucose from liver glycogen, and when glucose is back to normal the normal level stops the alpha cells (negative feedback).

items: Positive: oxytocin and contractions build up until birth. Negative: insulin (high glucose) and glucagon (low glucose) are switched off when glucose is normal.
